About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Geography Years 11–13 of the New
Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being published
separately.

Progress and assessment information for Geography Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Geography Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Geography Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students are taught how people, places, and environments are connected at local,
national, and global scales. Students examine how people’s relationships with the
environment are shaped by both natural processes and human activities and how
different perspectives influence understanding and decision-making about geographic
issues and challenges.

Geography provides students with the knowledge and practices to investigate people,
places, and environments and the connections between them. Students develop the
ability to analyse spatial patterns and processes, evaluate geographic issues and
responses, and communicate evidence-based conclusions about environmental and
societal challenges using geographic concepts and geospatial tools.

As students progress through Geography Years 11–13, they are taught to deepen
their ability to investigate, interpret, analyse, and draw conclusions from geographic
information and evidence. This enables them to evaluate issues from different
perspectives, assess impacts, and responses, and make informed judgements about
geographic questions and challenges.

 In Geography, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to analyse, evaluate, synthesise, and communicate geographic understanding using evidence, geographic
 concepts, terminology, and conventions to explain issues, justify judgements, and propose informed responses.

At Year 13, schools must provide opportunities for students to undertake a complete
geographic investigation within a single geographic context. Investigations should
broadly relate to a context encountered within the Physical or Human Geography
strands and should enable students to integrate geographic knowledge and practices
to develop a well-reasoned understanding of a geographic issue, process, pattern, or
relationship. Schools should select contexts that are authentic, locally relevant where
possible, and appropriate to the available time and resources. Students should
develop the aim, question or hypothesis, and methodology for their investigation with
teachers providing feedback on the investigation plan before students independently
collect, process, present, analyse, evaluate, and report on the investigation.
Examples of suitable contexts for the geographic investigation that support the
development of the knowledge and practices outlined in the earlier parts of the Year
13 teaching sequence include:
• beach processes and landforms

• beach mitigation and adaptation strategies

• vulnerability of a coastal environment

• the sustainability of strategies used to address water insecurity in a specific place

• trans-boundary water conflicts in a local area

• climate change in the local area.
